## Introduction

Zooplankton in the San Francisco Estuary (SFE) serve as a vital link between aquatic primary producers and higher trophic level consumers. As primary consumers of phytoplankton, zooplankton facilitate the flow of carbon through the large and complex SFE food web (Schroeter et al. 2015; Kimmerer et al. 2018; Hartman et al. 2025) that historically supported abundant fisheries. Zooplankton in the SFE are a key food source for endangered fish species, notably the Delta Smelt (*Hypomesus transpacificus*) and Longfin Smelt (*Spirinchus thaleichthys*) (Hobbs et al. 2006; Slater and Baxter 2014). Many species of fish, including Striped Bass (*Morone saxatilis*) and Chinook Salmon (*Oncorhynchus tshawytscha*) feed on zooplankton as larvae and juveniles (Goertler et al. 2018; Heubach et al. 1963), while others like Northern Anchovy (*Engraulis mordax*), Tule Perch (*Hysterocarpus traskii*), Prickly Sculpin (*Cottus asper*), Threadfin Shad (*Dorosoma pentense*), and American Shad (*Alosa sapidissima*) include zooplankton in their diets throughout their lifetimes (Kimmerer 2006, Feyrer et al. 2003). Changes in zooplankton abundance and community composition have been linked to major declines in pelagic fishes in the upper estuary (Baxter et al. 2008; Sommer et al. 2007; Winder and Jassby 2011).

The importance of zooplankton in the estuarine food web prompted implementation of the Zooplankton Study in 1972 to assess prey resources available to fish in the upper SFE. The study is mandated by the State Water Resources Control Board’s Water Right Decision 1641 and conducted jointly by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and the California Department of Water Resources under the guidance and management of the Interagency Ecological Program. For over five decades this study has monitored the zooplankton community in the region, tracking abundance trends and distribution patterns, detecting and monitoring introduced species, and documenting dramatic shifts in community composition.

This report presents zooplankton annual abundance indices from 1974 through 2025 and monthly abundance, biomass, and distribution trends from October 2024 through December 2025 for the most common copepods (calanoid and cyclopoid), cladocerans, rotifers, and mysids of the upper estuary.

## Methods

Zooplankton have been sampled in the upper SFE since 1972, once or twice per month from March to November through 1994, and monthly from 1995 to the present. Sampling was modified due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with no surveys in April and May 2020, a reduced survey (five stations) in December 2020, and no surveys in January and February 2021. Samples were collected at stations from San Pablo Bay through the Delta (Figure 1), including up to four non-fixed stations representing the low salinity zone (LSZ), defined as bottom specific conductance of 2 and 6 millisiemens per centimeter (approximately 1 and 3 psu). As of June 2024, sampling was suspended at stations 2 and 4 (Carquinez Strait), 325 (San Pablo Bay), and low-salinity zone stations in the San Joaquin River, but this sampling may be reinstated in the future.

Zooplankton were sampled using three gear types that target different size classes: 1) pump samples (collected with a 1/10 hp, 12V utility pump) filtered through a 43-micron mesh net for micro-zooplankton (rotifers, copepod nauplii, and small cyclopoid copepods); 2) Clarke-Bumpus (CB) net with 160-micron mesh to sample meso-zooplankton (cladocerans and most juvenile and adult calanoid copepods); 3) mysid net with 505-micron mesh targeting mysid shrimp and other macro-zooplankton. The mysid and CB nets were mounted on the same tow sled and samples were collected in 10-minute stepped oblique tows over the depth range of each station. Start and end counts from a General Oceanics flowmeter mounted in the mouth of each net were used to calculate volume filtered. Pump samples filtered 19.8 gallons (75 liters) over the upper 30’ of the water column; volume measured with an inline meter.

All zooplankton samples were preserved immediately after collection in 10% formalin with rose bengal dye. Target organisms in each sample were identified and counted in the laboratory using dissecting microscopes. More information about sampling and processing methods is in the metadata [here](https://filelib.wildlife.ca.gov/Public/IEP_Zooplankton/).

Catch per unit effort (CPUE) for all samples was calculated using the volume of water filtered during a net tow or pump sample. For pump samples this is the volume from the inline meter.  For net tows volume filtered was calculated as:

$$V=(endmeter−startmeter)k∗a$$\
where V is the volume of water sampled (mL), k is the flow meter constant, and a is the area of the mouth of the net (m^2^).

The pump samples 19.8 gallons over the upper 30’ of the water column, filtered through a 43-micron mesh net. All zooplankton samples are preserved immediately after collection in 10% formalin with rose bengal dye. Target organisms in each sample are identified and counted in the laboratory using dissecting microscopes. More information about the sampling and processing methods can be found in the metadata [here](https://filelib.wildlife.ca.gov/Public/IEP_Zooplankton/).

Abundance indices were calculated for each organism from its target gear type (noted above). Abundance is reported as mean CPUE, calculated as the number of each organism collected per cubic meter of water sampled:

$$CPUE=s∗V^{−1}$$\
where *s* is the estimated count of the target organism in the sample.

Annual indices comprise data from the 16 core stations sampled consistently since 1974 (Figure 1) and the two LSZ stations not in the San Joaquin River. Note that the number of LSZ stations per survey varied as only one sample was collected when the LSZ location was the same as a fixed station. Monthly indices combine data from all stations in the region, including LSZ stations when applicable. Calanoid and cyclopoid copepod indices comprise adults only, as juveniles cannot always be identified to species.

To analyze long-term trends (1974 to present), annual abundance indices were calculated as the mean CPUE for samples collected from March through November, as winter sampling was inconsistent before 1995. Monthly abundances span the period from October 2024 through December 2025 to encompass both water year and calendar year and are shown by region, as detailed in each section below. Estuary regions were designated as San Pablo Bay (stations D41, D41A), Suisun and Grizzly Bay (stations D6, 28, 48), Suisun Marsh (stations 32, S42), Confluence (stations 54, 60, 64, 74), Central Delta (stations D16, 86, D28, M10), North Delta (68), and South Delta (92) (Figure 1). Non-fixed LSZ stations were assigned to a geographic region based on their location. In 2025 these stations were mostly in the Confluence region (17 of 20), in Suisun and Grizzly Bay twice (March, May), and in Carquinez Strait once during the period of high outflow in February (Figure 2).

Biomass of copepods, cladocerans, and rotifers was determined following standard methods (Bashevkin et al. 2022 and references therein) using literature values of carbon per individual (Dumont et al. 1975, Salonen and Latja 1988, Uye et al. 1983, Culver et al. 1985, Sabatini and Kiørboe 1994, Uye and Sano 1995, Walz 1995, Kimoto et al. 1986, Logerwell and Ohman 1999, Hooff and Bollens 2004). For mysid biomass, dry weight was calculated based on length and converted to carbon using a standard conversion of 40% (Wiebe et al. 1975, Kiørboe 2013). Since mysid biomass depends on lengths of individual animals, a CPUE with no corresponding BPUE occurred either when an animal was not in good enough condition to measure or when CPUE was so low that BPUE was essentially zero. Monthly biomass indices for October 2024 to December 2025 were reported by region as biomass per unit effort (BPUE, calculated using volume filtered as for CPUE) in units of milligrams carbon per cubic meter of water (mgC m^-3^) for the most abundant species in the estuary.

## 2025 Conditions

Freshwater outflow was elevated from October 2024 through March 2025 with a period of intense high outflow in February 2025 (Figure 2). This high outflow event likely drove some zooplankton abundance and distribution patterns, which are discussed in detail below for each zooplankton group.

## Trends

The overall abundance of zooplankton in the estuary has decreased over the course of the Zooplankton Study (Figure 3). Cyclopoid copepods as a whole were the only group that increased in abundance over the study period, but this was driven by the introduction and proliferation of the invasive *Limnoithona tetraspina* in the mid-1990s. The overall decrease in zooplankton abundance can be attributed to invasive species colonizing the estuary, most notably the Asian clam *Potamocorbula amurensis* in the mid-1980s (Kimmerer et al. 1994; Carlton et al. 1990; Greene et al. 2011). Abundances of both phytoplankton and zooplankton in the upper estuary have been impacted by the proliferation of *P. amurensis*, as it is a highly efficient filter feeder and consumes phytoplankton and small zooplankton, including copepod nauplii. In addition to decreased abundance of most zooplankton groups, community compositions have changed dramatically during the study period (Figure 3), driven by a combination of the introduction and spread of non-native species and changes in the abiotic and biotic environments.

### Calanoid copepods

Aside from a 25-year high in calanoid copepod abundance in 2017, total annual abundance was similar from 1995 to 2025 (Figure 3). Total abundance of calanoid copepods in 2025 declined slightly compared to 2024 but remained within the range of the past seven years (2018-2024) with similar proportions of *Pseudodiaptomus forbesi* and *Acartiella sinensis,* the two most abundant species(Figure 3). Adult calanoid copepod abundance declined only slightly over the study period, but their community composition changed dramatically (Figure 3). When the study began in the early 1970s, the calanoid copepod community was dominated by *Acartia* spp. and an introduced *Eurytemora* (identified initially as *E. affinis* (Esterly 1924) but now considered *E. carolleeae* (Alekseev and Soussi 2011) and referenced in this report as *Eurytemora* spp.). Even though *Eurytemora* spp*.* is not native, it was once the primary prey of the endangered Delta Smelt. However, as its abundance declined, fish increasingly preyed on more recently introduced calanoids like *P. forbesi* (Moyle et al. 1992; Slater and Baxter 2014).

One of the first recorded calanoid copepod introductions was *Sinocalanus doerrii*, a freshwater species native to China that invaded the estuary in 1978 and remained the most dominant calanoid species for a decade (Orsi et al. 1983). The calanoid *P. forbesi* was first detected by this study in October 1987 (Orsi and Walter 1991), shortly after the *Potamocorbula amurensis* invasion in the mid-1980s (Carlton et al. 1990, Kimmerer et al. 1994). Combined effects of these introductions may have influenced subsequent abundance declines of *E. affinis* and *S. doerrii*. *P. forbesi* quickly became the numerically dominant calanoid in the upper estuary and remains the most abundant to this day. The predatory calanoid copepod *Acartiella sinensis* was introduced in 1993 and soon became the second most abundant calanoid in the upper estuary, dominating the low-salinity zone in the Suisun Marsh and Confluence regions (Orsi and Ohtsuka 1999). This invasion appears to have narrowed the range of *P. forbesi* towards freshwater areas of the estuary, likely due to *A. sinensis* predation on *P. forbesi* nauplii (Kayfetz and Kimmerer 2017).

Calanoid abundance and biomass, including *Eurytemora* spp., were very low in most upstream regions (South, Central, and North Delta, and Confluence) from January through March 2025, though there was a slight increase in *Eurytemora* spp. in the South Delta in March (Figure 4). This contrasts with seasonal distribution patterns from drought years (2020 through 2022) when *Eurytemora* spp. was the most common calanoid in these regions in spring ([previous reports here](https://github.com/emp-dwr/emp-website/tree/main/admin/archive/zoop)).

Similar to recent years, *Pseudodiaptomus forbesi* was the most common calanoid in the upper estuary (South Delta, Central Delta, North Delta, Confluence), but abundances remained low until May or June 2025 (Figure 4). This is similar to 2024 but differs from earlier years when abundances increased starting in March ([previous reports here](https://github.com/emp-dwr/emp-website/tree/main/admin/archive/zoop)). *P. forbesi* was abundant in the North Delta in May and June but calanoids were low in all other months in this region. In the Confluence and Suisun Marsh, *P. forbesi* abundance increased in May and June but declined starting in July, coincident with increasing abundance of *Acartiella* (Figure 4). In 2025 *P. forbesi* was abundant in Suisun Marsh from March through August, in contrast with low abundances in this region during the drought years from 2020 through 2022 ([previous reports here](https://github.com/emp-dwr/emp-website/tree/main/admin/archive/zoop)). *P. forbesi* inhabits low salinity waters so this species is typically rare in downstream regions but from May through August it was fairly abundant in Suisun Marsh and was present in Suisun and Grizzly Bays (Figure 4). Similar to 2024 ([previous reports here](https://github.com/emp-dwr/emp-website/tree/main/admin/archive/zoop)), *P. forbesi* was essentially absent from San Pablo Bay (Figure 4).

The predatory *Acartiella sinensis* was rare in the upper estuary and abundances were generally low in the Confluence, Suisun Marsh, and Suisun and Grizzly Bays from January through June 2025. Starting in July, *A. sinensis* was the most abundant species in the Confluence and Suisun Marsh, though it co-occurred with *P. forbesi* in most months (Figure 4). The Suisun Marsh calanoid community was approximately half *A. sinensis* and half *P. forbesi* in July and August, but both species declined sharply in September and remained low through December, with *A. sinensis* comprising most of the copepod community (Figure 4). *A. sinensis* was the most abundant species in Suisun and Grizzly Bays in all months except April (*Tortanus*), May (*Eurytemora*) and June (P*. forbesi*) (Figure 4). In these three regions, *A. sinensis* co-occurred with high densities of *Limnoithona tetraspina*, one of its primary prey items.

*Acartia* spp. were the only native calanoids commonly found in 2025. These copepods prefer brackish water and were present only in the lower estuary. They were the most abundant calanoids in San Pablo Bay, though monthly abundances varied (Figure 4, San Pablo Bay not sampled in March). In Suisun and Grizzly Bays, *Acartia* spp. were present during most months but abundant only in December 2024 and January and March 2025. In April and May, *Eurytemora* spp. were abundant in Suisun Marsh and moderately abundant in Suisun and Grizzly Bays (Figure 4). *Tortanus* spp. were present in Suisun and Grizzly Bays and San Pablo Bay throughout the year (Figure 4), similar to 2024 (emp-website/admin/archive/zoop at main · emp-dwr/emp-website · GitHub).

Biomass patterns followed CPUE patterns for all calanoid taxa except *Tortanus* spp. Although *Tortanus* spp. were rarely the most abundant calanoids, they were dominant in terms of biomass in Suisun and Grizzly Bays from March through September and in San Pablo Bay in February and May (Figure 4). These non-native predatory copepods are much larger than others with which they co-occur, making them a potentially more valuable food resource for fish.

### Cyclopoid copepods

In contrast with the decline of most major zooplankton groups during the study period, adult cyclopoid copepods increased dramatically, particularly from 2012 to 2022 (Figure 3). Cyclopoid copepods declined in 2023, likely due to downstream transport of these small organisms by high freshwater outflow (Figure 2) but abundances in 2025 were similar to 2024 (Figure 3).

Abundances of *Oithona* spp. and *Acanthocyclops* copepods were very low when the study began (Figure 3), and the increase in cyclopoid abundance resulted from the introduction of *Limnoithona sinensis* in the early 1980s and subsequent identification of the invasive *Limnoithona tetraspina* in 1993 (Ferrari and Orsi 1984; Orsi and Ohtsuka 1999). These two species were reported together as *Limnoithona* spp. from 1980 through 2006. *Limnoithona* were identified to species starting in 2007, leading to the discovery that *L. tetraspina* is by far the dominant species. For the sake of consistency, abundances were combined and reported here as *Limnoithona* spp. In 2025, *Limnoithona* spp. was by far the most abundant copepod group collected by this study (Figure 3).

The increase in *L. tetraspina* abundance may be related to decreased predation due to the decline of Northern Anchovy in the upper SFE (Kimmerer 2006). In addition, the small size, high growth rate, and motionless behavior of *L. tetraspina* may decrease its vulnerability to predation in a region where most fish are visual predators (Bouley and Kimmerer 2006, Kimmerer 2006). The introduction of *L. tetraspina* is linked to *P. forbesi* distribution shifting upstream of the low-salinity zone of the estuary, as higher densities of *L. tetraspina* may sustain larger populations of the predatory *A. sinensis*, which also preys on *P. forbesi* nauplii (Kayfetz and Kimmerer 2017).

*Limnoithona* spp*.* were the most abundant cyclopoids in 2025, but their abundances were generally low from January through May in all regions of the estuary and remained low in the South, Central, and North Delta in comparison with other regions (Figure 5). *Limnoithona* spp. abundances increased in the Confluence, Suisun Marsh, and Suisun and Grizzly Bays starting in May or June and remained high through November (Figure 5). In previous years *Limnoithona* spp. have been virtually absent from San Pablo Bay but were moderately abundant here from April through August, then declined with increasing salinities, concurrent with increased abundance of the introduced *Oithona davisae,* typically the most abundant cyclopoid in this region (Figure 5).

Biomass patterns followed CPUE for *Limnoithona* spp. and *Oithona* *davisae*, while BPUE of “other” cyclopoids was higher compared to CPUE (Figure 5) as this group includes some larger taxa. Cyclopoids in the “other” category may provide a valuable food source for fish, but not a consistent one due to low abundance and sporadic distribution (Figure 5). The “other” cyclopoids may have been an important addition to the food web in the North Delta in August when their biomass (27 mgC m^-3^) (Figure 5) augmented that of total calanoids (185 mgC m^-3^) (Figure 4).

### Cladocerans

Cladocerans in the upper estuary, primarily species in the genera *Bosmina*, *Ceriodaphnia, Daphnia*, and *Diaphanosoma*, declined substantially during the study period (Figure 3). Although there has been somewhat of an increasing trend since the late 1990s, abundances in 2025 were among the lowest of the study period, similar to 2011 (Figure 3). Cladocerans are largely herbivorous and feed primarily on phytoplankton, so were likely impacted by the proliferation of invasive copepods like *P. forbesi* (Orsi and Walter 1991). Throughout the upper estuary, cladocerans comprise a significant portion of Delta Smelt and juvenile Chinook Salmon diets (Slater and Baxter 2014; Goertler et al. 2018) and were historically an important food source for young-of-the-year Striped Bass (Heubach et al. 1963). Increased abundances of invasive copepods such as *P. forbesi* and the declines in native cladocerans may alter the nutritional content of the planktonic prey available to fish (Kratina and Winder 2015).

In the early years of the study, the cladoceran community was dominated by *Bosmina longirostris* and *Daphnia* spp. (Figure 3). Starting in 2013 the cladoceran community shifted to higher proportions of *Ceriodaphnia* spp. and *Diaphanosoma* spp., although *B. longirostris* and *Daphnia* spp. were still present (Figure 3). In 2025, total cladoceran CPUE (15,830) was less than half that of 2024 (38,470), with *Diaphanosoma* spp. the most abundant taxon, followed by low abundances of *B. longirostris, Daphnia,* and *Ceriodaphnia* (Figure 3). Abundance of the “other” cladocerans (CPUE 1362) was too low to register on the graph.

The Zooplankton Study detected a species of cladoceran new to the SFE in 2025. Known as the Baltic long nosed water flea, *Bosmina (Eubosmina) coregoni* is native to Eurasia. It has become established in the Great Lakes (Lieder 1991) and was likely present in watersheds in Oregon and Washington as early as the 1960s (Armstrong et al. 2025) but not detected until 2012 (Smits et al. 2013). To our knowledge, detection by the Zooplankton Study is the first record of *B. coregoni* in California. In the SFE, *B. coregoni* was found from February through November 2025 in all regions except San Pablo Bay, where salinity is likely too high for this freshwater species. Although it is widely distributed throughout the upper estuary, its abundance is low compared to bosminids as a whole. The Zooplankton Study reprocessed CB samples from previous years to determine *B. coregoni* abundance and first detection (to date February 5, 2024 in the Confluence region). At the time of this writing, *B. coregoni* has not been detected in samples from 2023. As this work is ongoing, *B. coregoni* is grouped with *B. longirostris* in this report. Preliminary work suggests that other nonindigenous bosminid species are also present in the estuary.

Although cladoceran CPUE in the South and Central Delta regions in 2025 was about one third that of 2024, the seasonal patterns were similar with low numbers in winter and spring followed by increased abundance in summer, with *Diaphanosoma* most abundant in the South Delta, and a combination of *Diaphanosoma*, *Daphnia*, *Ceriodaphnia*, and *Bosmina* in the Central Delta (Figure 6).

There was a distinct February peak in cladoceran abundance in five regions (North Delta, Confluence, Suisun Marsh, Suisun and Grizzly Bays, San Pablo Bay), with similar species composition (*B. longirostris, Ceriodaphnia, Daphnia*, “other”) in all regions except San Pablo Bay (Figure 6). These peaks, which were two- to ten-fold higher than February 2024, suggest that the high flow event in February 2025 (Figure 2) transported cladocerans downstream. The February peak in San Pablo Bay comprised *Ceriodaphnia* and *Daphnia* (Figure 6), freshwater taxa that do not usually occur in this region. This anomalous occurrence of freshwater taxa is consistent with transport from upstream by high outflow. In all other months, only “other” cladocerans were found in San Pablo Bay, with highest abundance in August 2025 (Figure 6).

Excluding the February peak, cladoceran abundances were lower in all regions in 2025 compared to 2024 (emp-website/admin/archive/zoop at main · emp-dwr/emp-website · GitHub), with the highest abundances in the South and Central Delta (Figure 6). (Note the difference in scale between the South and Central Delta compared to other regions, e.g. South Delta CPUE in October 2025 is similar to maximum CPUE in the North Delta and Confluence and much higher than maximum CPUE in Suisun Marsh, Suisun and Grizzly Bays, and San Pablo Bay). In the South and Central Delta, relatively low abundances of cladocerans in the early months of the year comprised *B. longirostris*, *Ceriodaphnia* spp., and *Daphnia* spp., plus the “other” category in March and April. Abundances were high from June through September with *Diaphanosoma* the most abundant taxon in both regions, along with *Ceriodaphnia* in the Central Delta from March through October. Although not abundant, *B. longirostris* was present in the South and Central Delta throughout 2025 (Figure 6).

Species composition and patterns of seasonal abundance were similar in the North Delta, Confluence, Suisun Marsh, and Suisun and Grizzly Bays, with highest abundances in the period from winter to early spring comprising *B. longirostris, Ceriodaphnia, Daphnia*, and “other” (Figure 6). Cladocerans were essentially absent from all regions except the North Delta from June through December, aside from low *Diaphanosoma* abundances in June in the Confluence and Suisun Marsh (Figure 6). In the North Delta, abundances were highest from December 2024 through March 2025, declined from April through June and remained low July through November, with *Diaphanosoma* present from May through October, and increased abundance in December comprising *B. longirostris* and the “other” category (Figure 6).

Biomass patterns followed CPUE for all taxa except *Daphnia* (Figure 6), which has higher biomass than other taxa with which it co-occurs, making it a potentially valuable food resource for fish, especially in the upper delta where it was present in most months in 2025.

### Rotifers

Although rotifers are the most abundant type of zooplankton in the upper estuary, their abundance decreased dramatically since the start of the study (Figure 3). Interestingly, the decline in rotifer abundance began in the late 1970s, preceding the invasion by *P. amurensis* (Cloern and Jassby 2012). The rotifer community comprised species from the genera *Polyarthra*, *Synchaeta*, *Keratella*, and *Trichocerca*, as well as the “other” rotifer category, which includes the genus *Asplanchna*. Aside from 2017, when rotifer abundances were similar to the late 1970s, rotifer abundance has been generally low since the early 1990s. Abundance increased in 2023 after several very low years but declined in 2024, when *Synchaeta* spp. abundance declined to about half that of 2023 (CPUE 5,864 and 11,502, respectively), and again in 2025, this time due to a decline in “other” rotifers (CPUE 1,362), in contrast with 2024 when “other” rotifers were the most abundant taxon (CPUE 8,158) (Figure 3). In 2025 *Synchaeta* spp. was the most abundant, followed by *Synchaeta bicornis* and *Keratella* spp. (Figure 3).

Similar to cladocerans, there were distinct regional peaks in rotifer abundances, likely driven by the high flow event in February (Figure 2). In the upper estuary (Central Delta, North Delta, Confluence, and Suisun Marsh), rotifer abundance (comprising *Keratella*, *Polyarthra*, and *Synchaeta* spp.) increased in February and spiked in March, while abundances increased in February in Suisun and Grizzly Bays and San Pablo Bay (Figure 7). *Keratella* and *Polyarthra* prefer freshwater and low-salinity habitats (Winder and Jassby 2011), and increased abundances of these taxa in the lower estuary are consistent with transport from upstream due to high flow. *Synchaeta* spp. co-occurred with them in all regions including San Pablo Bay.

Similar to previous years, a spatial and temporal split was discernible between *Synchaeta* and the other rotifer groups, with *Synchaeta* spp. the dominant group in the North Delta, Confluence, Suisun Marsh, Suisun and Grizzly Bays, and San Pablo Bay during winter and spring months but largely absent after April except in San Pablo Bay. *S. bicornis* was the most abundant taxon in September in the Confluence and Suisun Marsh, and from July through September in Suisun and Grizzly Bays, though *Synchaeta* spp. were also present and were more abundant than *S. bicornis* from October through December. The “other” rotifers group was most abundant in the Central Delta during summer. In the South Delta, extremely high abundance of *Synchaeta* spp. in November 2024 was followed by low abundances (less than 6,000) in this region throughout 2025 (Figure 7), in contrast with abundances over 20,000 in most months in 2024 (emp-website/admin/archive/zoop at main · emp-dwr/emp-website · GitHub).

Biomass patterns followed CPUE for all taxa except *Keratella*, which have lower individual biomass, and *Polyarthra*, which have higher individual biomass compared to abundance (Figure 7). These taxa both prefer freshwater habitats and co-occurred in all regions, but *Polyarthra,* even at lower abundances, are likely to provide a more beneficial food source for fish.

### Mysids

Mysid annual abundances were higher overall during the first 12 years of the Zooplankton Study, with the highest abundance in 1986 (Figure 3). From 1987 to the present, annual abundances have varied from 2.1 to 29.4 (mean 12.6), with the 2025 annual CPUE of 13.5 lower than 2024 (20.1) but similar to 2023 (13.1) (Figure 3), and still slightly higher than the mean over this period. In addition to an overall decline since the inception of the study, the mysid community composition shifted dramatically. Prior to 1994, the native *Neomysis mercedis* was the most abundant species but since 1994 the mysid community has been dominated by the introduced *Hyperacanthomysis longirostris* (formerly *Acanthomysis bowmani*) (Figure 3). *N. mercedis* declined significantly during the 1976-1977 drought, likely related to food limitation from a lack of diatoms due to low river discharges (Siegfried et al. 1979; Cloern et al. 1983). *N. mercedis* populations rebounded after the drought and abundances remained high in the Suisun Bay region until the introduction of *P. amurensis* in the mid-1980s, after which numbers declined dramatically and remained low (Orsi 1999). Consistent with previous years, the mysid community in 2025 was dominated by *H. longirostris*, followed by a small percentage of *Neomysis kadiakensis*. *H. longirostris* remained the most common mysid in the upper estuary, while the abundance of the once dominant native species *N. mercedis* remained extremely low, continuing the overall trend in mysid community composition since 1994.

The introduced mysid *H. longirostris* was first detected by this study in 1993, shortly after the decline of *N. mercedis*. Although *H. longirostris* quickly became the most common mysid in the upper estuary, total mysid abundances did not return to their pre-clam (*Potamocorbula amurensis*) invasion levels (Modlin and Orsi 1997, Figure 3). Historically mysids were critically important in the diets of many fish species in the upper SFE, including Delta Smelt, Longfin Smelt, Striped Bass, and Chinook Salmon (Moyle et al. 1992; Feyrer et al. 2003; CDFG 2009; Goertler et al. 2018). The decline of mysids in the upper estuary led to a significant decrease in their presence in fish diets (Feyrer et al. 2003).

In 2025 mysids were essentially absent from the South Delta, Central Delta, North Delta, and Confluence from January through April and abundances in other regions were low during this period (Figure 8). Mysids of any species were rare in the South Delta, Central Delta, and North Delta throughout the year. These are also the regions where the native *N. mercedis* was found, although in very low numbers.

*H. longirostris*, the dominant mysid, was the most common species in all regions except San Pablo Bay. It was abundant in the Confluence in May and June, in Suisun Marsh from April through October, and in Suisun and Grizzly Bays from May through July (Figure 8). Interestingly, *H. longirostris* had a spike in abundance in the South Delta in August (Figure 8), similar to 2024 but a much lower abundance (emp-website/admin/archive/zoop at main · emp-dwr/emp-website · GitHub). *Neomysis kadiakensis*, the second most abundant mysid species, co-occurred with *H. longirostris* in the Confluence from July through November, in Suisun Marsh from July through October, in Suisun and Grizzly Bays from May through July, and in San Pablo Bay in June, the only month when *H. longirostris* occurred in this region (Figure 8). *N. kadiakensis* also occurred in San Pablo Bay at low abundances in February, June, July, September, November, and December (Figure 8).

The “other” mysid species (*Acanthomysis aspera, Acanthomysis hwanhaiensis, and Alienacanthomysis macropsis*) typically comprised the San Pablo Bay community, though this group was also present in Suisun and Grizzly Bays with higher salinities from September through December. The “other” mysids were present in San Pablo Bay in most months (not sampled in March), though abundances were very low aside from June and September (Figure 8). Note that the Zooplankton Study samples only the upper portion of San Pablo Bay, so these findings do not represent the mysid community in other areas of San Pablo Bay.

Note that the “other” group comprised three species of mysids so biomass varied depending on species composition. Biomass patterns followed CPUE for all mysid species except *N. kadiakensis*, where biomass was higher compared to abundance (Figure 8). Their larger size, combined with their presence in most months in regions from the Confluence to San Pablo Bay, makes them a potentially valuable prey resource for fish.

## Conclusion

In 2025, the Zooplankton Study recorded copepods, cladocerans, rotifers, and mysids at abundances consistent with the historic downward trends in the upper estuary. Zooplankton biomass comprised mainly calanoid copepods (38%) and rotifers (33%), followed by cyclopoid copepods (23%), cladocerans (6%), and mysids (\<1%). Rotifer abundances peaked in March, while abundances of all other zooplankton groups peaked in summer of 2025. High freshwater outflow in February 2025 likely transported small zooplankton from upstream into lower estuary regions, resulting in low numbers of these taxa in upstream regions. The small, introduced cyclopoid *Limnoithona tetraspina* remained the most abundant copepod in upper estuary regions (North, South, and Central Delta), though its BPUE in these regions was low compared to calanoids, cladocerans, and rotifers. Mysid abundance remained low compared to historic levels and decreased slightly in 2025 compared to 2024. The mysid community remained dominated by the introduced *Hyperacanthomysis longirostris,* in comparison to the pre-1987 community, which was dominated by the native *Neomysis mercedis*.

The long-term Zooplankton Study allows researchers and managers to track shifts in zooplankton abundances and community composition in the upper estuary over more than five decades. The Zooplankton Study has documented the introduction and dominance of *Pseudodiaptomus forbesi*, *Limnoithona tetraspina*, and *Hyperacanthomysis longirostris*, the community’s response to the invasive clam *Potamocorbula amurensis,* and is uniquely positioned to monitor the zooplankton community for impacts of the recent invasion of the SFE by golden mussels(*Limnoperna fortunei*) and the introduction of *Bosmina longirostris*. Understanding these dynamics and how they have fundamentally changed trophic interactions is critical to assessing conservation strategies and food resources for fish in the upper San Francisco Estuary.
